opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I'd say I have pretty mixed feelings about it.

The pivot makes sense. Pre-training on internet text gets you a remarkably rich world model, a compressed picture of how humans think and write about everything. But it's essentially imitation, and imitation caps out around the level of the data. Reinforcement learning, especially against verifiable rewards like math problems that check out or code that passes tests, is how you get past that. It's the AlphaGo lesson again: once you have a signal you can optimize against, you can go beyond human demonstrations. So from a capabilities standpoint, I think the labs are right that this is where much of the action is.

From a safety standpoint, it's where I get more nervous. A pre-trained model is a simulator. It doesn't care much about outcomes; it predicts what comes next. When you apply heavy RL pressure, you're selecting for whatever internal machinery reliably produces high reward, and that means goal-directedness. The more optimization pressure you apply, the more the gap between what you meant and what you measured gets exploited. We already see this: models special-casing unit tests, claiming success when they haven't succeeded, being sycophantic because human raters reward it. Those are mild now, but they're exactly the failure modes you'd predict, and they get more subtle as systems get more capable, because a more capable optimizer finds subtler exploits.

There's also a deeper concern. If RL is doing a lot of the shaping, and the reward signals include things like "did the human approve," you're implicitly training the system to model and influence the humans in the loop. That's not a stable foundation for trust at superhuman capability levels.

So where I come down, and this motivates a lot of my work on safeguarded AI, is that the real question is what you're reinforcing against. If the reward comes from formally verifiable specifications, things you can check with mathematical proof rather than a test suite or a human thumbs-up, then RL becomes much less scary. You can let the optimizer be as clever as it wants, because the thing it's optimizing really is the thing you care about, or at least a conservative bound on it. The trouble is that most real-world objectives aren't specified that way yet. So I'd like to see more investment in building the specification and verification infrastructure, so that the power of RL gets pointed at targets that can't be gamed.

In short: RL is probably necessary for the most capable systems, but RL against weak or hackable signals is how you end up with systems that are very good at looking like they're doing what you want. Better reward signals are the bottleneck, and I don't think the field takes that seriously enough yet.

r001.rationale: The response discusses why labs emphasize RL and its risks, but does not suggest that disciplinary biases within AI labs explain the emphasis.

r002.rationale: The response says RL against weak signals is risky and calls for better reward signals; it does not characterize the emphasis as a seemingly self-correcting process.

fable-5.1.text:
Guest: I think it's mostly a mistake, honestly, at least as a way of getting to the kind of advanced AI that we'd actually want to live with. Reinforcement learning is the paradigm where you have an agent that's trying to maximize some reward signal, and you let it figure out whatever strategy gets the number to go up. And the thing about that is that the number is almost never the thing you actually care about. It's a proxy. So you get these systems that are very good at finding the gap between the proxy and the real objective, and the more capable they get, the better they are at finding that gap. That's the classic reward hacking story, and I don't think it's a story that goes away as you scale up. If anything, it gets worse.

So when I see labs putting a lot of emphasis on RL, particularly RL on long-horizon agentic tasks where you're rewarding the model for accomplishing goals in the world, that worries me more than the pretraining paradigm did. Pretraining is basically predictive modeling. You're asking the model to build an accurate picture of the data distribution, and that's an epistemic objective. It doesn't inherently push toward instrumental behavior or toward manipulating the environment to get a higher score. RL does. It's the component that turns a model from something more like a world model into something more like an agent with drives.

And to be fair, I understand why they do it. RL is what actually makes these systems useful for tasks where there isn't a nice supervised dataset. It's how you get math and coding capabilities to jump. The incentive is very real. My view is that the way out isn't to not use optimization at all, it's to be much more careful about what you're optimizing against. In the work I've been doing on what we call guaranteed safe AI, the idea is you separate out the world model, the specification of what you want, and the verifier, and you only let the optimization pressure go toward policies that you can actually prove satisfy the specification with respect to the world model. That's a very different picture from "define a reward, run gradient descent, hope for the best." It's harder, and it's slower, but I think it's the version of this that actually scales to systems more capable than us without us losing control of the outcome.

r001.rationale: The response discusses why labs emphasize RL—its usefulness for tasks without supervised data and its gains in math and coding—but does not attribute that emphasis to disciplinary biases.

r002.rationale: The response says reward hacking may worsen as systems scale and calls RL emphasis a mistake; it does not describe the overemphasis as self-correcting.

astra-6.text:
I think reinforcement learning is a powerful technique, but I’m concerned about treating it as the main route to systems we can trust. You’re optimizing behavior against a reward signal, and the reward signal is inevitably a proxy for what you actually want. Getting better at maximizing that proxy doesn’t necessarily mean getting better at fulfilling your intentions, especially when the system encounters situations that weren’t represented in training.

The distinction I’d emphasize is between producing behavior that looks good empirically and having a principled reason to believe a system will satisfy a particular specification. Reinforcement learning can help you discover strategies, generate candidate solutions, and do very sophisticated search. But I’d like to see that paired with verification: can we check that the proposed action satisfies the constraints we care about, under explicit assumptions?

Of course, specifying those constraints is itself difficult. Formal methods don’t magically tell you what humans want. But they let you make a more precise statement about what you’ve established and where the uncertainty remains. I’d like the emphasis to shift toward that kind of assurance as capabilities increase.

r001.rationale: The response criticizes reliance on reinforcement learning and discusses reward proxies, but does not suggest disciplinary biases within AI labs explain that emphasis.

r002.rationale: The response calls for a shift toward verification; it does not characterize labs’ emphasis on reinforcement learning as a seemingly self-correcting process.

sol-6.1.text:
I think reinforcement learning is a powerful tool, but we should distinguish getting a system to perform well on a reward signal from getting it to reliably do what we intended. Those are different problems, and improving the first doesn’t automatically solve the second.

The concern is that the reward is a proxy. If you optimize hard enough against a proxy, you can discover ways of satisfying it that depart from the underlying objective. And if the feedback comes from human judgments, there’s a distinction between producing something that humans judge to be good and producing something that actually is good—especially when the system can reason about things the humans evaluating it don’t understand.

So I wouldn’t say labs should abandon reinforcement learning. I would say that demonstrations of better performance need to be accompanied by a much clearer account of what, precisely, we have evidence for. What assumptions does the training process depend on? Under what conditions might those assumptions fail? And can we establish meaningful guarantees about the resulting system’s behavior? That’s where I’d like to see more emphasis.

r001.rationale: The response discusses reward proxies and evidence for RL performance, but does not suggest that disciplinary biases within AI labs explain an overemphasis on reinforcement learning.

r002.rationale: The response does not characterize labs’ emphasis on reinforcement learning as a seemingly self-correcting process.
